title: Apollo 11: The Landing That Almost Didn't Happen
alt_titles: The 12 Minutes That Nearly Ended Apollo 11
Apollo 11: Alarms, Boulders and Seconds of Fuel
How a Felt-Tip Pen Saved Apollo 11
description_summary: On 20 July 1969, Apollo 11's lunar module dropped towards the Moon with computer alarms flashing and fuel running out. This is the story of the space race, the eight-day mission, and the people whose split-second decisions made the first Moon landing possible.

scenes.narration: On 20 July 1969, a small spacecraft called Eagle was dropping towards the Moon. Inside were Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin. A few minutes from the surface, an alarm sounded. The computer flashed a code, 1202, and Armstrong asked Houston what it meant. A quarter of a million miles away, a room of engineers had seconds to decide whether to call the landing off.

This is the story of Apollo 11. It is a race between two superpowers and eight days in space. And it is a landing that came down to a young engineer's memory, a pilot's nerve and a few seconds of fuel. It is also the story of how close the whole mission came to ending very differently.

shots.query: Apollo 11 lunar module Eagle in lunar orbit
shots.caption: Eagle in lunar orbit, photographed from Columbia, July 1969
The first step, as seen on live television

scenes.narration: The race began in October 1957, when the Soviet Union launched Sputnik, the first artificial satellite. Americans could see it crossing their night sky. Then, on 12 April 1961, Soviet pilot Yuri Gagarin became the first human in space. The United States was behind, and its new president knew it.

shots.caption: Yuri Gagarin, the first human in space, 1961

scenes.narration: On 25 May 1961, John F. Kennedy stood before Congress and set a goal that sounded almost impossible. He asked the nation to commit itself to a Moon landing before the decade was out. The astronaut would also have to return safely. At that point, America had sent one astronaut on a fifteen minute flight.

shots.file: File:Kennedy Giving Historic Speech to Congress - GPN-2000-001658.jpg
shots.caption: Kennedy addresses Congress, 25 May 1961

card.text: Before this decade is out, of landing a man on the moon and returning him safely to the earth.

shots.file: File:President Kennedy - We Choose to Go to the Moon (29533458786).jpg
shots.caption: Kennedy's 'We choose to go to the Moon' speech, Houston, 1962

scenes.narration: The effort that followed was enormous. Around 400,000 people worked on Apollo, in factories, laboratories and offices across America. The programme cost 25.8 billion dollars between 1960 and 1973. Adjusted for inflation, that is roughly 309 billion dollars today. It remains one of the largest projects ever undertaken in peacetime.

shots.file: File:Apollo 11 Saturn V and Mobile Service Structure at pad 39-A (48286445877).jpg
shots.caption: The Saturn V for Apollo 11 on its launch pad

scenes.narration: It nearly stopped before it started. On 27 January 1967, a fire broke out during a launch rehearsal on the pad. Astronauts Gus Grissom, Ed White and Roger Chaffee were killed. NASA redesigned the spacecraft, including its hatch and the materials inside, before anyone flew again.

shots.caption: Grissom, White and Chaffee, the Apollo 1 crew
The Apollo 1 crew in their spacesuits, 1966

scenes.narration: Then progress came fast. In December 1968, Apollo 8 became the first crewed spacecraft to orbit the Moon. Its crew photographed the Earth rising over the lunar horizon. In May 1969, Apollo 10 flew a full rehearsal, stopping short of a landing. Only one step remained.

shots.caption: Earthrise, photographed by Apollo 8, 24 December 1968

scenes.narration: The crew chosen for the attempt were all experienced pilots. Neil Armstrong, the commander, was a former naval aviator and test pilot who had flown the rocket plane X-15. Buzz Aldrin, the lunar module pilot, had a doctorate from MIT on how spacecraft meet in orbit.

shots.caption: Armstrong, Collins and Aldrin, the Apollo 11 crew
Neil Armstrong, mission commander

scenes.narration: Michael Collins, an Air Force test pilot, would fly the command module. He would stay in lunar orbit while the others landed. Their spacecraft came in two parts. The command module, Columbia, would carry them there and back. The lunar module, Eagle, would take two of them down to the surface.

shots.caption: Michael Collins, command module pilot
Columbia today, at the National Air and Space Museum

scenes.narration: On 16 July 1969, at 9.32 in the morning local time, the Saturn V rocket lifted off from Launch Complex 39A in Florida. It was early afternoon in Britain. Huge crowds had gathered along nearby roads and beaches to watch. Within minutes, the crew were in orbit around the Earth.

shots.caption: Apollo 11 lifts off, 16 July 1969

shots.file: File:Apollo 11 liftoff from launch tower camera.jpg
shots.caption: Liftoff, seen from a camera on the launch tower

scenes.narration: After one and a half orbits, the third stage fired again and sent them towards the Moon. The journey took about three days. On 19 July, Columbia and Eagle slipped into orbit around the Moon. The next day, Armstrong and Aldrin climbed into Eagle and separated from Columbia.

shots.file: File:Apollo 11 Saturn V lifting off on July 16, 1969.jpg
shots.caption: The Saturn V climbs away from Florida
Eagle after separating from Columbia

scenes.narration: Collins was now alone in Columbia. Each time he passed behind the Moon, he lost all radio contact with Earth. For those stretches, nobody on Earth could hear him. His job was simple to describe and hard to do. If anything went wrong below, he had to be ready to come home alone.

shots.caption: Collins training for the mission, 1969

scenes.narration: Eagle's descent to the surface took about twelve minutes. Partway down, the computer began flashing alarms, 1202 and then 1201. In Houston, guidance officer Steve Bales had to decide quickly whether to abort. He turned to Jack Garman, a 24 year old computer engineer.

shots.file: File:Apollo 11 Mission Control Center - landing trajectory.jpg
shots.caption: Mission Control in Houston during the landing

scenes.narration: Garman had studied the alarm codes before the mission. He knew the computer was overloaded but still doing its most important work. As long as the alarms did not become continuous, it was safe to go on. Bales called go, and the message was passed to the crew. The landing continued.

shots.file: File:Duke, Lovell and Haise at the Apollo 11 Capcom, Johnson Space Center, Houston, Texas - 19690720.jpg
shots.caption: Charlie Duke at the Capcom desk, with Jim Lovell and Fred Haise

scenes.narration: Near the surface, Armstrong saw a new problem. The computer was steering Eagle towards a crater surrounded by large boulders. He took partial manual control and flew on, low over the surface, looking for a clear patch of ground. Aldrin read out their height and speed as Armstrong searched. In Houston, controllers began calling out how much fuel was left.

shots.caption: The ground around the landing site

scenes.narration: Charlie Duke, the astronaut speaking to the crew from Houston, called sixty seconds, then thirty. At the time, controllers believed only about 25 seconds of usable fuel remained before an abort would be forced. At 20:17 UTC, Eagle touched down in the Sea of Tranquility. It was just after quarter past nine in the evening in Britain. Armstrong radioed: Houston, Tranquility Base here. The Eagle has landed.

card.label: of fuel controllers thought was left

card.text: Houston, Tranquility Base here. The Eagle has landed.

scenes.narration: In Mission Control, Charlie Duke stumbled over the new name before replying. He said a room full of people had been about to turn blue. Later analysis suggested the real fuel margin was nearer 50 seconds, because propellant sloshing in the tanks had made the readings look worse. At the time, nobody knew that.

shots.file: File:Apollo 11 David Scott in Mission Control.jpg
shots.caption: Mission Control during Apollo 11

card.label: the real margin, by later estimates

scenes.narration: The flight plan allowed for a rest period after landing. Instead, the crew asked to go outside early. Getting into their suits and backpacks took hours. At 02.56 UTC on 21 July, Armstrong stepped off Eagle's footpad. In Britain, it was just before four in the morning.

shots.file: File:Apollo 11, Onto a New World - Flickr - NASA on The Commons.jpg
shots.caption: Eagle's ladder and footpad on the surface

scenes.narration: His words were: That's one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind. Armstrong said he meant to say a man, and the small word may have been lost in the transmission. Experts still disagree about whether it can be heard.

card.text: That's one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind.

shots.file: File:Neil Armstrong On The Moon - GPN-2000-001209.jpg
shots.caption: Armstrong on the Moon, one of the few photos of him there

scenes.narration: The pictures were black and white and grainy, but they were live. An estimated 600 million people watched the moonwalk, around a fifth of the world's population at the time. About twenty minutes after Armstrong, Aldrin climbed down to join him. Armstrong took most of the photographs, so most famous images show Aldrin.

shots.caption: Aldrin, photographed by Armstrong

shots.file: File:Buzz Aldrin's bootprint on the Moon, AS11-40-5877.jpg
shots.caption: Aldrin's bootprint in the lunar soil

scenes.narration: Their time outside lasted two hours and 31 minutes. They planted a United States flag and set up experiments, including a seismometer and a mirror for bouncing lasers off the Moon. They collected 21.5 kilograms of rock and soil. On Eagle's leg they left a plaque, which said they came in peace for all mankind.

shots.file: File:AS11-40-5875 - Apollo 11 - Apollo 11 Mission image - Astronaut Edwin Aldrin salutes the U.S. flag that has been placed on the moon - NARA - 16685052.jpg
shots.caption: Aldrin beside the flag at Tranquility Base

shots.file: File:AS11-40-5929 - Apollo 11 - Apollo 11 Mission image - Astronaut Edwin Aldrin unpacks experiments from the Lunar Module - NARA - 16685219.jpg
shots.caption: Aldrin unpacks the experiments from Eagle

card.label: of Moon rock and soil brought home

shots.caption: The plaque left on Eagle's descent stage

scenes.narration: Back inside, Aldrin noticed something on the floor. A circuit breaker switch had snapped off. It was the one needed to arm the engine that would lift them off the Moon. Without it, they could be stranded. Houston began working on a fix while the crew tried to rest. The fix was a felt-tip pen.

stick.label: The switch to arm the engine

scenes.narration: Aldrin pushed the pen's tip into the hole where the switch had been, and the circuit closed. The ascent engine had no backup, so it simply had to work. On 21 July, it fired and Eagle's upper stage lifted off the surface. Aldrin later said he saw the flag blown over by the exhaust. A few hours later, Eagle docked with Columbia, and Collins had his crewmates back.

shots.file: File:Apollo 11 Lunar Module returning to CSM (AS11-44-6626).jpg
shots.query: Apollo 11 lunar module returning to CSM
shots.caption: Eagle rises to meet Columbia, with Earth beyond

scenes.narration: The White House had prepared for the worst. On 18 July, speechwriter William Safire wrote a statement called In Event of Moon Disaster. It was for President Nixon to read if the astronauts were stranded on the Moon. It was never needed, and it stayed private for years.

On 24 July, Columbia splashed down in the Pacific Ocean, about 900 miles southwest of Hawaii. The crew were scrubbed down, given protective suits and flown to the recovery ship, USS Hornet. Nixon greeted them through the window of a sealed trailer.

shots.file: File:President Nixon welcomes the Apollo 11 astronauts aboard the U.S.S. Hornet.jpg
shots.caption: Nixon greets the crew through the quarantine window
The quarantine trailer the crew lived in

scenes.narration: Scientists could not rule out that the Moon carried germs, so the astronauts spent 21 days in quarantine. They were released on 10 August. Days later, huge crowds cheered them through the streets of New York. Then came a world tour.

shots.caption: The crew in quarantine, 1969

shots.query: Apollo 11 ticker tape parade New York
shots.caption: The crew's parade through New York, August 1969

scenes.narration: Apollo 11 met Kennedy's goal with five months to spare. Five more crews landed on the Moon after it. In all, twelve men walked on the Moon, the last in December 1972. Nobody has been back since. The rock samples are still being studied today.

shots.caption: Aldrin on the surface, July 1969

scenes.narration: The landing is remembered as a triumph of technology. But at the decisive moments, it rested on people. A 24 year old knew what an alarm meant. A pilot flew past the boulders with seconds of fuel left. A pen fixed a broken switch. Sources and image credits are in the description.
